excerpt: A file is one document. A folder holds files. Learn where your work is kept, how to save it under a name you will still understand later, and how to find it again.

body.text: This lesson shows you where your work lives after you type it. You will learn what a file is, how to save it with a name you will still understand next year, and how to find it again. If you have ever lost work you typed, this lesson is the answer to that fear.

A file is one complete piece of work: a letter, a picture, a form, a song. A folder is a container that holds files. Most people do not lose documents because computers are difficult. They lose them because nothing was ever given a name.

body.alt: A file window showing the Documents, Pictures and Desktop folders.
body.caption: Each yellow icon is a folder. Double-click one to open it, and look at the address bar at the top to see where you are.

body.text: Before you start

items: A computer with about thirty minutes free.
One document you do not mind practising with.
Nothing else. You do not need to buy a flash drive today.

body.text: If the machine belongs to someone else, ask before you save anything. Then use a folder with your own name, so that nothing of theirs is touched.
The folders you already have
Open File Explorer on Windows, the yellow folder on the taskbar, or Finder on a Mac. Five folders are already there, and each one has a job.

items: Desktop: things you are using today. Easy to reach, and easy to fill with clutter.
Documents: letters, forms, school work, anything you write.
Pictures: photographs and saved images.
Downloads: files the internet sends you. A delivery mat, not a store room.
Recycle Bin or Trash: files you deleted. They stay there until you empty it.

body.text: You will see these folders every time you open the window, so there is no need to memorise them today. Use Documents for anything you write, and the habit will hold.
Make one folder for each part of your life
A good folder structure answers one question quickly: where would I look for this in six months? Keep it shallow, because deep nests of folders hide files from the person who made them.

items: Open Documents.
Right-click an empty space, choose New, then Folder.
A yellow folder appears with its name highlighted and ready to type over.
Type School and press Enter.
Open School and make folders inside it, such as Fees and Certificates.
Do the same once for Work and once for Personal, then stop.

body.text: It looks like a folder called Misc is tidy. By December it is a hiding place, because you cannot remember what you put inside it. Name the folder for what you will be looking for, not for how you feel today.
Save a file where you can find it
Until you save, your work exists only in the open window. If the light goes, it is gone. Saving copies the work onto the disk, where it stays even with the machine switched off.

items: Type one sentence in Word, Notepad, or Google Docs.
Press Ctrl and S together. On a Mac, press Command and S.
The first time, a window asks for a name and a place.
Choose Documents, then the folder you made.
Name the file with the subject and the month, such as school-fees-march-2026.
Press Save.

body.text: You will see the folder name change in the address bar at the top of the window, and the file appear in the list. That change is the proof that the work is now on the disk and not only on the screen.
Do not worry about getting the perfect name on the first try. You can rename a file by right-clicking it and choosing Rename, and a clear name an hour later beats a perfect name you never saved.
Save again, and save a copy
From now on, Ctrl and S updates the same file without asking questions. Press it every few minutes while you write, and a power cut costs you the last minute instead of the afternoon.
Save As makes a new copy under a new name. Use it when you want to keep the old version and begin a new one. Save school-fees-march, then use Save As to create school-fees-april.
It looks like final, final2, and latest-final are careful names. They tell a reader nothing, and even you will not know which one is true in three months.

body.alt: A laptop keyboard with hands resting on the home row.
body.caption: Ctrl and S, pressed often, is the cheapest insurance in computing. It takes a second and saves an afternoon.

body.text: If it goes wrong
None of these means the work is lost for good, so read them without alarm.

items: You cannot find the file: open Documents, then the folder you remember, then check Downloads.
You closed the window without saving: the work is gone, because it was never copied to the disk. This is the one case saving cannot fix, which is why Ctrl and S matters.
The file is in the Recycle Bin: right-click it and choose Restore. It returns to the folder it came from.
You saved over the wrong version: open the program and look for a list of recent versions, or restore the older copy from your backup.
The computer asks to save when you close: read the three buttons before you click. Save keeps it, Don't Save discards it, Cancel keeps the window open.
The file will not open on another computer: save and send a PDF instead of the editable file.

body.text: Practice
Fifteen minutes on this today and you will never lose a document the same way again.

items: Make a folder called Practice inside Documents.
Write two sentences, save them inside Practice as my-first-file, and close the window.
Open the file again from File Explorer and add one sentence.
Delete the file, then restore it from the Recycle Bin.
Search for the file by typing part of its name, and open it from the results.

body.text: You can now save work so that it survives a power cut, and find it months later. That is a skill most people are still learning at fifty. In the next lesson your hands will learn to type without hunting for every key.

excerpt: Where to rest your fingers, which keys fix mistakes, and the shortcuts that save hours. Ten minutes of practice a day is enough to stop hunting for letters.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to type without hunting for every key. You will learn where to rest your fingers, how to fix mistakes quickly, and the shortcuts you will use every day. If your typing is slow today, that is normal, and it is also temporary.
Typing is a physical skill, like riding a bicycle. Reading about it does not make you faster. Your hands learn the positions by doing them slowly, and speed arrives on its own once accuracy is there.
Before you start

items: A computer with a keyboard and about twenty minutes.
A chair that lets your feet rest on the floor.
No need for a typing program. Notepad is enough.

body.text: Sit, then place your hands
Before you type a word, set up your body. A bad position is why many people blame the computer for back and wrist pain after an hour of work.

items: Sit upright with both feet flat on the floor.
Keep the screen at eye level, about an arm's length away.
Bend your elbows at about ninety degrees and drop your shoulders.
Rest the four fingers of your left hand on A, S, D, and F.
Rest the four fingers of your right hand on J, K, L, and the key beside L.
Rest both thumbs on the long bar at the bottom.

body.text: Feel the small raised line on the F and J keys. You will see that these two keys feel different from the rest, and that is on purpose. The bumps let you find your place without looking down, even in a dark room.

body.alt: Two hands resting on a laptop keyboard in the home row position.
body.caption: Left fingers on A, S, D, F. Right fingers on J, K, L and the key beside L. Thumbs on the space bar.

body.text: The eight keys under your fingers are called the home row. Every other key is reached from there and then your fingers come back. Keep them there between letters, and the keyboard stops feeling like a field you have to search.

The first week will feel slower than the way you type today. That is normal, because your old way has years of practice behind it and this one has none. Give it ten minutes a day and the positions will stop needing thought.
The keys that fix mistakes
Most trouble at the beginning comes from pressing the wrong editing key, not from a broken machine. These are the ones worth knowing on the first day.

items: Enter or Return finishes a line and starts a new one.
Backspace removes the letter before the cursor.
Delete removes the letter after the cursor, or deletes a selected item.
Space bar leaves one space between words. Press it once, not three times.
Shift gives a capital letter, or the symbol above a number key.
Caps Lock types every letter in capitals until you press it again.
Tab jumps to the next box in a form, or indents a line.

body.text: If every letter comes out in capitals, Caps Lock is on. You will see a small light on the key itself, or a symbol on the screen, depending on the laptop. Press the key once and carry on. If you have typed a whole line that way, select it and press Ctrl and Z.
It looks like your fingers are the problem when a line comes out wrong. It is usually the position: a thumb resting on the trackpad moves the cursor, and the next letters land somewhere else.
Five shortcuts that save time
A shortcut is two keys pressed together. It does the same job as a menu, with fewer steps and without moving your hand to the mouse.

items: Ctrl and C copies what you selected.
Ctrl and V pastes the copy where the cursor is.
Ctrl and X cuts, which moves the selection instead of copying it.
Ctrl and Z undoes your last action.
Ctrl and S saves the file.

body.text: On a Mac, use Command in place of Ctrl. The letters stay the same, so Command and C copies and Command and Z undoes.
To select text, click at the start of a word, hold the button down, and drag to the end. You will see the text change colour, and that colour is how the computer knows what you mean.

body.alt: A learner typing on a laptop with a document open on the screen.
body.caption: Select first, then copy. The text turns a different colour when the computer knows what you mean.

body.text: If it goes wrong
None of these means the keyboard is broken, and all of them are common in the first week.

items: Letters appear in the wrong place: you clicked somewhere else in the text. Click where you want the cursor, or press Ctrl and Z.
Every letter is a capital: press Caps Lock once.
A key repeats and fills the line: the key is stuck. Press it firmly a few times, or switch the keyboard.
The cursor jumps while you type: your palm is touching the laptop trackpad. Move your hands back or turn the trackpad off.
You typed a line into the wrong box: select it, press Ctrl and X, click the right box, then press Ctrl and V.
Your wrists ache: stop for the day, and raise the chair or the screen so your wrists stay straight.

body.text: Practice
Ten honest minutes a day beats a course you never open.

items: Type the home row letters, left hand then right hand, ten times without looking down.
Type your full name ten times, using Shift for each capital letter.
Type a sentence, press Ctrl and Z twice, then type it again.
Write the same short sentence for ten minutes a day for one week.
At the end of the week, count your mistakes. Aim for fewer, not for faster.

body.text: You can now find the home row by touch, fix a mistake without panic, and use the shortcuts most office work depends on. In the next lesson you will reach the internet and find what you need without getting lost.

excerpt: How to open a browser, tell the address bar from the search box, use tabs, read a web address, and save a page you will want again. Simple habits that prevent most mistakes.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to use the internet on purpose. You will open a browser, search for what you need, keep several pages open, and check that a site is really the one you wanted. Nothing here requires you to be technical, and nothing here can break the computer.

The internet is a very large library with no librarian and no locked door. Anyone can put a page on the shelf, including people who want your password or your money. Most of this lesson is about knowing which shelf you are standing at.
Before you start

items: A computer connected to Wi-Fi or data.
A browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari.
About twenty minutes, and one thing you actually want to look up.

body.text: Open the browser and read the screen
The browser is the program you use to visit pages. All of them work the same way, so learning one is enough.

items: Click the browser icon on the taskbar, or search for Chrome or Edge in the Start menu.
Find the long box at the top. That is the address bar.
Type an address you know, such as cea.ng, and press Enter.
Read the address once the page has loaded, and check it is the place you asked for.
Use the left arrow at the top left to go back one page.

body.text: You will see the page begin to load, sometimes with a progress line in the tab, then the content fill in. On a slow connection the text may appear before the pictures, and that is normal.
The address bar can also search. If you type words it does not recognise, it sends them to a search engine. That is convenient, and it is also how people arrive somewhere they never intended to go.

body.alt: A young man searching on a laptop at a small table with a phone beside him.
body.caption: The address bar is the top box. Read it before you trust a page, because it shows the real owner of the site.

body.text: Ask a search engine a real question

A search works when the question is specific. Computer is a warehouse. How to save a Word document on Windows 11 is a shelf. Put the thing you want and the situation you are in into the same sentence.
You will see a list of results, each with a title, a short description, and a small grey address under it. That grey address is the one to read, because it says who published the page.

Add the word Nigeria when the answer depends on where you are, such as JAMB registration deadline Nigeria. Read the grey address under each result before you click it. A result from waec.org.ng is not the same as a blog that mentioned WAEC once.

The first results are often adverts, marked Ad or Sponsored. They paid to be there, which does not make them wrong, but it does mean they are selling. Scroll to the results that are not marked and choose the one that seems to answer your question.
Use tabs instead of losing your place
A tab is a page you keep open while you look at another. The row of small titles at the top is the tab bar, and the plus sign opens a new one.

items: Click the plus sign to open a new tab.
Type a different address or search in the new tab.
Click a tab title to switch back to that page.
Click the small X on a tab to close only that page.
Right-click an empty part of the tab bar and choose Reopen closed tab if you closed one by mistake.

body.text: It looks like a closed tab is lost. It usually is not. The browser remembers recently closed pages, and one right-click brings them back, which is why a mistake here costs a second rather than a morning.

body.alt: A laptop on a desk showing a browser with several tabs open.
body.caption: Five bookmarks you use every week are worth more than fifty you saved and forgot.

body.text: Check a site before you trust it
A small padlock beside the address means the connection is private, so nobody on the network can read what you send. It does not mean the owner is honest. A thief can rent a padlock too.

items: Read the address slowly and look for spelling tricks, such as gtbank-help.com instead of gtbank.com.
If the browser shows a red warning that the connection is not private, do not type a password there.
If a page asks for bank details and you arrived from a link in a message, close it and type the address yourself.
If a page says your computer is infected, close the tab. That message is usually an advert for a fake repair.
If a download starts without asking, close the tab and check Downloads before opening anything.

body.text: Downloads land in your Downloads folder. Move a file into Documents if you mean to keep it, and save a page with the star at the end of the address bar. Give the bookmark a name you will recognise, not the machine's suggestion.
If it goes wrong
The internet fails in a few ordinary ways, and every one of them has a next step.

items: The page will not load: check the Wi-Fi or data connection, then press the reload button once.
Every page is slow: close the tabs you are not using, then try again.
You cannot find a page you had open: right-click the tab bar and choose Reopen closed tab.
The page is asking for money or a card: leave it, and reach the organisation through its own address.
You downloaded something by accident: open Downloads, delete the file, and do not open it first.
A page keeps opening on its own: close the tab, then check the browser for extensions you did not add.

body.text: Practice
Do this with one real question in mind, so the practice produces something you actually needed.

items: Open your browser and type cea.ng in the address bar.
Open two more tabs and search for something you needed to know today.
Use Back to return to the first result list, then switch tabs by clicking the titles.
Save the page you use most often as a bookmark.
Check the address of every page you open for the next ten minutes before typing anything into it.

body.text: You can now reach a page, search for what you need, keep several pages open, and check where you really are. In the next lesson you will use those skills to send your first email.

excerpt: An address, a subject that tells the truth, a short body with one job, and the paperclip. How to write and send a first email that a school or office will answer.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to send an email that looks like a person wrote it on purpose. You will fill To, Subject, and the message, attach a file, and know when to use Reply instead of Reply all. If email makes you nervous, that is common, and it gets easier after the second one.

Email is a letter that arrives in seconds. WhatsApp is faster, but schools, banks, and employers still ask for email because it keeps a record. A message sent by email can be found a year later, along with the file that came with it.

body.alt: A laptop showing an email being written with To, Subject and a message body.
body.caption: Three fields decide whether the mail works: To, Subject, and the body. Read all three before you press Send.

body.text: Before you start

items: An email address of your own, written down.
A second address you can open, such as a family member's, for the practice mail.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Write your own address in a notebook now. People lose work because they forget their own address, create a second one, and then check the wrong inbox. One address, written down, is enough for years.
Nothing in this lesson can reach a stranger if you read the address before you send. And if something does go wrong, one short follow-up message fixes it, and nobody remembers it a week later.
Fill the three fields in order
Open Gmail, Outlook, or the Mail app and click Compose or New mail. Fill the fields from the top down, so that you never finish a letter and then send it to the wrong person.

items: To: type the other person's address exactly. One wrong letter sends the mail to a stranger or to nobody.
Subject: write the label the reader will see in a list of fifty. Application for Computer Basics, September is a subject. Hello is not.
Body: click the large empty space and write the letter.
Check the address and the subject once more before you type a word.

body.text: You will see the address turn into a small name in a box once the mail program recognises it. If it stays as plain text, read every letter again before you continue.

A body that works here and anywhere else has four parts. Greet the person by name. Say in one sentence why you are writing. Say in one sentence what you want them to do. End with your full name and a phone number.
It looks like a long letter shows seriousness. It usually shows that the writer did not decide what they wanted. One clear request gets answered, while four questions get a reply to the last one.
Send a practice mail

items: Open Gmail or Outlook in the browser.
Click Compose.
Put a trusted address in To, such as a family member or a second address of your own.
Subject: Practice mail from your name.
Body: Good morning. This is a practice message. My name is your name. My number is your number.
Click Send, then open the other inbox and confirm the mail arrived.

body.text: You will see a short message at the bottom of the screen saying the mail was sent, and the mail will appear in your Sent folder. If the message says it is sending and the window closes, the mail is still on its way, so no need to send it again.
Attach a file correctly
An attachment is a file that travels with the letter: a receipt, a passport photograph, a filled form. Look for the paperclip icon and click it.

items: Choose the file from Documents, Desktop, or Downloads.
Wait until the file name appears under the body, or a small box shows the upload finished.
Check the name. school-fees.pdf tells the reader what it is. IMG_0048 tells them nothing.
Send a PDF when the file is a document, so it looks the same on the other person's computer.
Keep the file under about 10 MB where you can. A photo straight from a phone camera is often larger.

body.text: If you write Please find attached, look under the body first. A mail that promises a file and carries nothing wastes a day, and the reader will not always tell you.

body.alt: An email with a paperclip attachment showing a PDF named school-fees.pdf.
body.caption: The paperclip means a file is coming. Check that the name is there before you press Send.

body.text: Reply, Reply all, and Forward

items: Reply sends your answer to the person who wrote to you.
Reply all sends it to everyone who received the original, which is wrong when thirty parents are on the list.
Forward sends the letter to a new person. Add one sentence at the top saying why.
Use Reply by default, and Reply all only when every person on the list needs your answer.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Email is forgiving. Almost every mistake here can be corrected with one more message.

items: The mail bounces back: one letter in the address is wrong. Compare it with the address the person gave you.
The attachment will not send: the file is too large. Send a link, or make the photo or PDF smaller.
You sent the mail to the wrong person: email cannot be recalled. Write again at once and say what happened.
No reply comes: wait a day, check Spam, then send one short follow-up rather than five repeats.
A stranger asks you to confirm a password by email: do not reply. No bank asks for a password by email.
The reply went to everybody on the list: apologise in one short line, and use Reply next time.

body.text: Practice
Two practice mails today will do more than an hour of reading.

items: Write your own address on paper and read it aloud to somebody.
Send a practice mail to a trusted address with a clear subject and your full name.
Attach one PDF or photograph to a second mail and check the name appears before you send.
Open your Spam folder and look at what a fake bank message looks like, without clicking anything inside it.

body.text: You can now write an email that is easy to answer, attach the right file, and avoid the two mistakes that embarrass people most. In the next lesson you will protect all of this with passwords you can actually keep.

excerpt: How to make a password you can remember, store it safely, and add a second lock to the accounts that matter. Includes what to do when someone gets in.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to make strong passwords, keep them somewhere safe, and add a second lock to the accounts that matter most. You will set one up today and build the habit over the next week. Forgetting a password is normal, and so is fixing it.
A password is a key. It should be long and hard for another person to guess, and it should be different for each important account. One copied key opens every door in the house.
Before you start

items: A notebook and a pen that stays at home.
Your phone, for the second lock.
About thirty minutes, because you will change one password properly.

body.text: What makes a password strong
Length matters more than symbols. A long phrase of ordinary words beats a short word with a capital letter and an exclamation mark, and it is far easier to remember.

items: Use at least twelve characters. Sixteen is better.
Join four unrelated words, such as mango-bicycle-lagos-cup.
Add a number you will not forget, but not your year of birth or phone number.
Never use your name, your child's name, your school, or 123456.
Never reuse the password from your bank on a shopping site.
Change a password at once if a company tells you its customer list was leaked.

body.text: P@ssw0rd is a common example of a password that feels clever and is not. Many people already use it, and a program can try it in less than a second.
Make one you can actually remember
A password you cannot recall at the school gate is a password you will replace with something weak. Build one around a sentence that belongs to you.

items: Think of a sentence you will not forget, such as my first shop opened near Ojo market.
Take four strong words from it in the same order: shop, Ojo, market, first.
Add a number and a capital letter: Shop-Ojo-Market-First-27.
Type it five times slowly on the real keyboard before you save it anywhere.
If the account asks for a symbol, add one at the end and write the exact version down.

body.text: It looks like a simpler password is kinder to yourself. In practice, the long phrase is easier to remember than P@ssw0rd27, because your mind already knows the sentence.

body.alt: A small notebook and pen beside a laptop keyboard.
body.caption: A paper notebook kept at home beats the same short password on twenty websites. Write the site, the name, and the password in the same order every time.

body.text: Where to keep the list
Nobody remembers twenty long passwords. You have two honest choices, and both are better than reuse.

items: A password manager, which stores them behind one master password.
A notebook that stays at home in a drawer, not in your bag and not on the office desk.
The browser's saved passwords, if the computer itself needs a password to start.

body.text: Never keep the list in a message to yourself on WhatsApp, in a draft email, or in a note called passwords on the desktop. If somebody takes the phone, those are the first three places they look.
Add the second lock
Two-step verification asks for your password and then one more proof, such as a code sent to your phone. A thief with your password still cannot get in without the second step.
You will see a screen offering a code by SMS or an app, and then a set of backup codes. Keep that window open until the codes are written on paper, because it shows them only once.
Turn it on for your email first, because email can reset every other account you own. Then do your bank and your school portal.

items: Open your email account settings and find Security.
Look for Two-step verification and turn it on.
Choose the code by SMS if you always have your number, or an authenticator app if your network is unreliable.
You will see a list of backup codes. Save them on paper, in the same drawer as the notebook.
Sign out of every device once, then sign in again with the new password.

body.alt: A phone showing a login screen with a verification code field.
body.caption: The code on the phone is the second lock. Nobody needs it except you, and no support desk will ask you to read it out.

body.text: What you never type into a surprise

items: A password on a page you reached from a link in a message, even if the page looks exactly like your bank.
A one-time code read out to someone who called you first. Your bank will not ask for it.
A password on a website without a padlock and an address you recognise.
Your login details in a reply to an email, however urgent the message sounds.
The same password on a small site you will never use again.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every item below is recoverable, and none of them means you are careless.

items: You forgot the password: use Forgot password on the real site, and reset through the email or phone number on the account.
Somebody has changed your password: use the recovery option, then check the recovery email and phone number are still yours.
You cannot receive the code: check the number on the account, restart the phone, and use a backup code if you saved one.
You typed the password into a page that felt wrong: change it now on the real site, and sign out of all devices.
The account is locked after several wrong tries: stop guessing and wait thirty minutes.
A site emails you a password in plain text: treat that account as weak, change the password, and do not use it for anything important.

body.text: Practice
One account today, one more each week, and within a month the risk has mostly gone.

items: Write down the three accounts that would hurt most to lose: email, bank, and school or work.
Make one long password for email and type it five times correctly.
Turn on two-step verification for that email account.
Write the password and the backup codes in the notebook and keep it at home.
List any website where you used that email password, and change those over the next seven days.

body.text: You can now build a password you can keep, store it without embarrassment, and put a second lock on the accounts that matter. In the next lesson you will meet the message that tries to steal the key.
